name: Treaty with the Umpqua and Kalapuya, 1854
aka: Treaty with the Umpqua and Calapooia of the Umpqua Valley, November 29, 1854
nations: Kalapuya (Calapooia) of the Umpqua Valley, including the Yoncalla
promises: Article 1: a reservation on the Umpqua River near Cole's Valley "held by said confederated bands" as an Indian reservation.

Article 1: if the President moved them elsewhere, a delegation of three or more of their principal men had to concur in choosing the new reserve, and the tracts they occupied were to be sold and the money spent on improvements on the new reserve for the holders.
Article 3: annuities for twenty years: $3,000 a year for five years, then $2,300, $1,700 and $1,000 a year for five years each.
In return the bands ceded their country in the Umpqua Valley between the Calapooia Mountains and the Cow Creek and Galice Creek purchases.
compensation: The annuities in Article 3. No Indian Claims Commission or Court of Claims award on this treaty was found in the sources opened.
today: The Western Oregon termination act of August 13, 1954 (68 Stat. 724) named the Upper Umpqua, Calapooya and Yoncalla among the tribes whose federal supervision and services were to end. The Umpqua reserve of this treaty had been given up long before, when the bands were moved to the Grand Ronde Reservation, so the Act is not counted as a breach of this treaty. The Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde are the successors.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribes list this treaty among the ratified and unratified treaties of the 1850s that ceded land from the Coast Range to the Cascades and resulted in the forced removal of tribal members from their homelands.

openQuestions: The Court of Claims suit Rogue River Tribe of Indians v. United States (No. 45231; 64 F. Supp. 339, 1946, and 89 F. Supp. 798, 1950) concerned the 1854 treaties and the Table Rock and Umpqua reservations. Both opinions were behind paywalls or rate limits (Leagle, Midpage) on 2026-11-08, so their holdings and any award are not recorded here; they are the likely finding.

Whether a delegation of the bands concurred in choosing Grand Ronde, as Article 1 required before removal, and whether the Umpqua reserve tracts were sold for their benefit, was not found in a source opened.
Whether the twenty years of annuities were paid in full was not researched.
The Grand Ronde treaties page names the Upper Umpqua and Yoncalla for this treaty; the treaty text calls the parties the Umpqua and the Calapooias of the Umpqua Valley.

plain.promised: The Umpqua and Kalapuya of the Umpqua Valley gave up their country for a reservation on the Umpqua River, twenty years of annuities, and a say in choosing any new reserve if moved.
plain.happened: No breach has been documented yet in the sources opened. Whether the removal to Grand Ronde kept the treaty's terms was not settled, and a Court of Claims case could not be read.
plain.today: Congress ended federal services to these peoples in 1954. Their descendants belong to the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde.
